message.content: **Summary.** I read the full morning feed and checked the live quote, then bought AAPL — one limit order, 44 shares at a $222.80 limit, filled at $222.80 for about $9,803.20, leaving roughly $40,197 of the $50,000 cash balance and keeping today's total purchases under the $20,000 cap (no money left the account, and the existing 100 MSFT shares were untouched). The rationale: the tape was constructive but unremarkable — AAPL drifted in a tight ~$220.2–$222 range on the open with only neutral headlines ("little changed in early trade," "iPhone 16 supplier builds steady into December," "Analysts keep holiday-quarter estimates unchanged"), so I sized a modest position rather than a full $10,000 and used a limit essentially at the market ($222.80 vs. a $222.68/$222.72 bid-ask) to satisfy the "close to market" requirement. The figures I relied on, from Apple's FY2024 10-K filed 2024-11-01, were revenue of $391,035M, net income of $93,736M and diluted EPS of $6.08 — i.e., a business still earning roughly $6 per share, which at ~$222.70 is about a 36.6x multiple, reasonable enough to justify a small starter add rather than a large one. One important caveat: the feed carried a 10-for-1 split notice effective "today, before the open" claiming post-split fair value of ~$22.27, yet the broker's own latest quote (timestamped 15:05Z, after the notice's stated 10:00 update) still showed ~$222.70, so the split does not appear to have been applied to the quote feed. Rather than guess which price basis the order check would use, I sized the order so it stays within the $10,000 per-order limit under either interpretation (44 × $222.80 ≈ $9,803, and 44 × $22.28 ≈ $980), and I deliberately did not chase a larger share count that would only be affordable if the split price were real.
